newsitem.title: INDIA: India in political limbo as Congress woos rival.
newsitem.headline: India in political limbo as Congress woos rival.

text.p: India's Congress party, keen to sidestep an early general election, said on Saturday it had no plans to seek power and would support the defeated United Front coalition if it replaced ousted Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda as leader.
In the latest twist to a political cliff-hanger, the Congress said it had no thirst for power after helping to topple Deve Gowda's centre-left government on Friday.
"If they come up with a new leader, we will support them," Congress spokesman Ved Prakash told Reuters by telephone in the Indian capital. "We will not press our claim to form the government."

Congress's entreaty appeared aimed at wooing the United Front and staving off a snap election which could strengthen the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), accused by rivals of favouring majority Hindus over the Moslem minority.
But there was no sign the United Front was ready to accept Congress's demand that Deve Gowda quit as coalition leader.
Congress chief Sitaram Kesri said his first priority was to avoid polls that could ensue if the United Front and Congress failed to agree on a successor to Deve Gowda.

Kesri told party members there was no question of going to the polls, he was not a contender for any office and Congress would support the United Front at the head of a new government if it named a new leader, the Press Trust of India said.
Congress leader A.K. Antony said: "I am not particular about Congress government. My priority is that secular forces should get together, and this is not a time for elections."

Undercut by Congress, Deve Gowda suffered a resounding defeat in a vote of confidence in parliament late on Friday and immediately submitted the resignation of his 10-month-old centre-left government to President Shankar Dayal Sharma.
Sharma asked Deve Gowda to remain as caretaker prime minister while efforts were made to forge a new governing majority in the hung parliament.
The confidence vote was triggered after Kesri withdrew his party's make-or-break support for Deve-Gowda's minority coalition on March 30.
After a two-hour meeting of its decision-making body, the United Front said it would stand by Deve Gowda.
"There is no question of supporting the BJP or Congress in forming a government," said United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy.
The coalition said it would refuse to help either Congress or the rightwing BJP to form a new government, and a senior official said fresh polls seemed almost certain.
But United Front and Congress leaders were engaged in backroom talks to keep the BJP, the largest group in the 542-member lower house with 162 deputies, from making a bid for power.
The Press Trust of India said cracks were appearing in the United Front, and some regional parties in the coalition were inclined to consider Congress's appeal to avert polls.
The United Front was to meet again to discuss strategy at 8 p.m. (1430 GMT) on Saturday, he said.
The BJP was holding its cards close to its chest, and said it was keeping all of its options open.

All political formations agreed on Friday to try to approve the 1997/98 (April-March) budget in a special sitting of parliament from April 21 to 23. That would give politicians almost two weeks to resolve differences over a new government.
